title: Neurologic Complications of Systemic Illness and Critical Care
summary: Systemic critical illnesses—especially sepsis, multiorgan failure, hypoxia, and metabolic derangements—are tightly linked to acute and chronic neurologic complications. High-value care focuses on early detection of encephalopathy and ICU-acquired weakness, prevention of delirium, meticulous avoidance of secondary brain injury, and structured neuroprognostication. Evidence supports protocolized delirium prevention, sedation minimization, glycemic safety, and early mobilization while recognizing prognostic uncertainty in the ICU.
clinicalQuestion: What neurologic complications arise from systemic critical illnesses, how should clinicians prevent, detect, and manage them in the ICU, and what are the key prognostic and systems-level considerations?

heroStats.label: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy
heroStats.value: Common; associated with ↑ mortality and long-term cognitive impairment [1], [8], [10]

keyMoments.title: Recognize early encephalopathy
keyMoments.body: Screen all critically ill patients for delirium and decreased arousal; evaluate for hypoxemia, sepsis, metabolic derangements, sedative accumulation, and nonconvulsive seizures [8], [9], [10].

keyMoments.title: Detect ICU-acquired weakness
keyMoments.body: Suspect critical illness polyneuropathy/myopathy when weaning failure or diffuse weakness occurs; perform bedside MRC sum score and consider NCS/EMG if persistent [8], [10], [11].

keyMoments.title: Prevent secondary brain injury
keyMoments.body: Optimize oxygenation, perfusion, glucose, temperature, and sedation; avoid deep sedation when possible and use structured delirium prevention bundles [10], [4], [5].

keyMoments.title: Structured prognostication
keyMoments.body: Time prognostic conversations appropriately; use multimodal assessments and avoid sedative confounding, especially after cardiac arrest and severe sepsis [7], [10].

keyMoments.title: Advance systems and equity
keyMoments.body: Implement multidisciplinary neurocritical care education, standardized quality indicators, and palliative integration to reduce disparities and improve outcomes [3], [4], [5].

sections.title: Major Neurologic Complications from Systemic Critical Illness
sections.blurb: Systemic inflammation, hypoxia, microvascular dysfunction, metabolic disarray, and iatrogenesis converge to impair the central and peripheral nervous systems.

steps.title: Sepsis-Associated Encephalopathy (SAE)
steps.body: Characterized by fluctuating inattention, altered arousal, and EEG slowing without overt CNS infection. **Mechanisms include cytokine-mediated neuroinflammation, endothelial dysfunction, BBB disruption, and mitochondrial injury.** SAE is linked to **higher mortality and long-term cognitive decline** [1], [8], [10].

steps.title: Delirium and Long-term Cognitive Impairment
steps.body: Delirium is common in ICU and predicts worse functional outcomes. **Risk is amplified** by benzodiazepines, deep sedation, sepsis, hypoxia, and metabolic abnormalities. Persistent cognitive deficits are reported months after discharge [10].

steps.title: ICU-Acquired Weakness (Critical Illness Polyneuropathy/Myopathy)
steps.body: Presents with diffuse, symmetric limb weakness and difficulty weaning from ventilation. **Risk factors:** sepsis, multiorgan failure, hyperglycemia, corticosteroids/neuromuscular blockers. EMG/NCS can differentiate neuropathy vs myopathy. Recovery may be prolonged [8], [10], [11].

steps.title: Hypoxic–Ischemic Brain Injury (HIBI)
steps.body: Follows respiratory failure, shock, or cardiac arrest. **Secondary injury** arises from reperfusion, edema, seizures, and dysautonomia. Neuroprognostication must avoid sedative confounding and is multimodal [7], [10].

steps.title: Metabolic/Toxic Encephalopathies
steps.body: Uremia, hepatic failure, hypo/hypernatremia, hypo/hyperglycemia, hypercapnia, and medication toxicity commonly precipitate encephalopathy or seizures. **Rapid correction of severe derangements is essential**, with careful avoidance of overcorrection (e.g., osmotic demyelination) [9], [10].

steps.title: Cerebrovascular Events Triggered by Systemic Illness
steps.body: Sepsis, DIC, AF, and ECMO can precipitate ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke through coagulopathy and embolism. Vigilance for focal deficits or unexplained coma is critical [9], [10].

steps.title: Iatrogenic/Sedation-Related Effects
steps.body: Benzodiazepines and deep sedation increase delirium and prolong ventilation. **Analgosedation strategies** and daily sedation interruption may mitigate harm [10].

sections.title: Prevention, Detection, and Management
sections.blurb: Prioritize early recognition and bundle-based prevention while individualizing diagnostic testing.

cards.title: Screening & Monitoring
items: Use RASS for arousal and CAM-ICU or ICDSC for delirium each shift [10].
Consider continuous EEG for persistent coma, fluctuating mental status, or suspected nonconvulsive seizures [10].
MRC sum score for strength when cooperative; trend handgrip or diaphragm ultrasound for weaning failure [10], [11].
Track glucose, sodium, ammonia, urea, PaCO2, thyroid/adrenal axes if unexplained encephalopathy [9], [10].

cards.title: Delirium Prevention Bundle
items: Promote daytime wakefulness: lights, mobilization, eyeglasses/hearing aids [10].
Minimize benzodiazepines; prefer dexmedetomidine/propofol for ventilated patients when appropriate [10].
Daily sedation interruption and spontaneous breathing trials when safe [10].
Sleep hygiene: noise reduction, clustered care, melatonin as institutional practice [10].

cards.title: ICU-Acquired Weakness Mitigation
items: Early mobilization and PT/OT when hemodynamically stable [10], [11].
Avoid persistent deep sedation and unnecessary NMBA exposure [10].
Maintain euglycemia; avoid both severe hyper- and hypoglycemia [10].
Assess nutrition and protein adequacy; address vitamin D deficiency per local protocols.

cards.title: Red Flags Requiring Escalation/Imaging
items: New focal deficits, acute severe headache, papilledema, or seizures [9], [10].
Coma unexplained by sedation, or asymmetric pupils/posturing [9], [10].
Rapid sodium shifts, hyperammonemia, or severe hypercapnia with altered mental status [9], [10].

cards.title: Diagnostic Workup Pearls
items: CT head initially for structural lesions; MRI for diffuse axonal injury, HIBI patterns, PRES, or encephalitis [9], [10].
LP when CNS infection suspected; do not delay antimicrobials in septic shock [9], [10].
EEG: diffuse slowing in SAE; triphasic waves in metabolic encephalopathy; look for nonconvulsive status [8], [10].
NCS/EMG: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy (CIP) vs myopathic MUAPs (CIM) [8], [11].

cards.title: Prognostication & Follow-up
items: Use multimodal approach: exam off sedation, EEG reactivity, SSEP, neuroimaging, and biomarkers when available [7], [10].
After cardiac arrest, defer final prognostication ≥72 h after normothermia and sedative clearance; avoid self-fulfilling bias [7].
Plan post-ICU cognitive and neuromuscular rehabilitation; screen for depression, PTSD, and cognitive impairment [10].

sections.title: Service Delivery and Equity in Neurocritical Care
sections.blurb: Structured neurocritical programs and quality indicators reduce variation and improve outcomes.

steps.title: Multidisciplinary Neuro-ICU Teaming
steps.body: Specialized units and trained teams **improve processes and outcomes**, but gaps persist in education, individualized therapy, and access in underserved regions [3], [5].

steps.title: Standardization and Quality Metrics
steps.body: Emerging quality indicators and consensus guidance target sedation, analgesia, hemodynamics, and neuromonitoring to **reduce complications and disparities** [4], [5].

steps.title: Palliative Integration
steps.body: Early palliative involvement aligns care with values, especially where prognostication carries uncertainty and potential long-term disability [3], [5], [7].
